Concrete Driveways · Sanford, FL

Pouring a Concrete Driveway in Sanford

A new concrete driveway in Sanford costs $6–$15 per sq ft installed as of October 2026. The city's LDR Schedule N sets the layout rules for anything touching the right-of-way: a $250 permit fee, at least 10 feet of separation from the neighbor's driveway, and an apron poured at 3,000 psi minimum.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

Schedule N sets the spacing before the forms go up

Three numbers from Sanford's Land Development Regulations drive most driveway layouts: a 10-foot minimum gap from the neighbor's driveway, a 35-foot clearance from the street's parallel pavement on a standard lot (smaller on a tight corner parcel), and 3,000 psi concrete for the apron itself (City of Sanford, LDR Schedule N). A driveway that also crosses an existing sidewalk pours that section 6 inches thick rather than the usual 4, since Schedule N treats a vehicular crossing differently from a plain walking surface. Getting any one of those figures wrong on the plan is what usually sends an application back for revision before it reaches the Citizenserve inspection queue.

Choosing a Finish Before the Truck Shows Up

A broom finish is the plain, standard surface most driveways get: a broom is dragged across the concrete while it is still workable, leaving a texture that sheds water and resists slipping. Exposed aggregate goes a step further, washing or blasting the surface cement off so the stone inside the mix shows through, which changes both the look and the grip underfoot. Both sit within the basic tier of finish work, well short of stamped or multi-color decorative treatments. The choice has to be made before the pour starts in Sanford, since a broom finish cannot become exposed aggregate after the fact without resurfacing.

Replacing an apron on a street the city maintains, worked out in square feet

Take a 22 by 24 ft two-car driveway, 528 sq ft, on a Sanford street inside the city's own right-of-way. At $6–$15 per sq ft installed, the job falls between roughly $3,168 and $7,920 before any demolition of the old slab is added in. Add the $250 city permit fee on top, and check the plan against Schedule N's 10-foot spacing from the neighbor's driveway before the forms go in, since a layout that's too tight to the property line is the single change order that shows up most often on a Sanford job once the survey comes back.

The $250 fee covers the city; a county road means a different office entirely

Sanford's own Article VII fee schedule lists the single-family residential driveway permit flat at $250, filed through the Building Division once the layout clears Schedule N (City of Sanford, LDR Article VII Fees). A lot that technically fronts a Seminole County-maintained road instead of a city street skips that fee and the Citizenserve queue entirely, routing instead through the county's own Residential Driveway Construction Application, with its own 18-foot width cap and 18-inch minimum culvert (Seminole County, Residential Driveway Construction Application). Confirming which office actually owns the road before ordering concrete avoids paying one fee and then being told to file with the other.

A Settling Driveway and a Sinkhole Aren't the Same Thing

Most cracked or uneven driveways are settlement, not sinkholes: a sign the base underneath was not compacted enough or that soil beneath the fill shifted over time. A true catastrophic ground cover collapse under Florida law involves a sudden, visible depression and structural damage, not a slowly widening crack at a control joint. Orange County sits on the state's broader list of counties with concentrated sinkhole claims; Sarasota and Manatee do not. Either way, a Sanford homeowner seeing gradual unevenness in a driveway is almost always looking at a compaction or drainage issue a contractor can diagnose, not a geological event that needs reporting to the state.

Ridge Sand Doesn't Behave Like Flatwoods Soil

The sand ridge soils west of Orlando, Candler, Astatula and Tavares, drain almost too well: the water table can sit more than 80 inches down. That sounds like easier ground to build on, but loose, excessively drained sand does not hold a compactor's pass the way a firmer soil does, and it can shift under the plate instead of locking together. On a ridge lot in Sanford, we wet the material enough to bind it, then compact in shallow lifts rather than one deep pass. Skip that step and the driveway can still settle later, just for the opposite reason a flatwoods lot would.

The Paperwork That Happens Before Anyone Touches a Shovel

On a job with a direct contract over $2,500, Florida law requires a Notice of Commencement recorded and posted before work actually starts, with permit cards carrying a warning that skipping this step can mean paying twice. For a Sanford homeowner, part of the process happens at a desk, not on the driveway: paperwork gets filed and the notice gets posted at the job site before the crew mobilizes. It has nothing to do with concrete chemistry and everything to do with protecting the homeowner's right to the property if a dispute ever comes up later.

Reading Rainy Season Numbers Before the Storms Start

Orlando averages about 51.45 inches of rain a year and Sarasota-Bradenton about 49.05, most of it concentrated in a rainy season that typically runs from late May into October. Before that season starts, it is worth walking a Sanford driveway and clearing leaves, mulch and sand out of the control joints, since a joint packed with debris cannot channel water the way an open one does. Standing water that collects against a slab edge because a joint is clogged works on the base underneath over an entire wet season, not just one storm, which is a slower version of the same settlement problem poor compaction causes.

Frequently asked questions

How much is a Sanford driveway permit?

$250 for a single-family residential driveway, published in the city's LDR Article VII fee schedule and filed through the Citizenserve portal (City of Sanford, LDR Article VII Fees).

How far apart do Sanford driveways have to be?

At least 10 feet from an adjacent driveway, with an additional rule requiring at least 35 feet from the street's parallel pavement, both reduced proportionally on a smaller corner lot (City of Sanford, LDR Schedule N).

What happens if my driveway fronts a county road instead of a city street?

The application moves to Seminole County's Development Review Division instead of Sanford's Building Division, using the county's own width and culvert rules rather than Schedule N (Seminole County).
